migrationNotes: Spine: two bakers, one quicker at everything. We price each cake in loaves, give each baker the job they give up less for, let them swap, find the prices that suit both, and test the idea with a pair whose costs match.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): econ-comparative-advantage-dev-check (Cleo and Dev). The same comparison is made in the Ana and Ben screens.
Teaching examples (potters Mo and Jo) differ from the practice examples (bakers, studio) so no screen gives away a later answer.

lesson.title: Who should make what

steps.headline: Counting one job in the other's output

lead.text: The last lesson priced a table in chairs. The same idea works for one person. A potter can make 9 bowls or 3 vases in a day, but not both. Nine bowls and three vases each fill the whole day, so one vase takes as long as three bowls. A vase costs the potter 9 ÷ 3 = 3 bowls.

The price reads the other way too. One bowl takes a third of the time of a vase, so a bowl costs 3 ÷ 9 = a third of a vase. Each good has a price in the other, and the two prices are upside-down versions of each other.
A price like this belongs to one person. A second potter with different daily totals has different prices, and the gap between them is what this lesson is about. First, here is a baker to price.

lead.text: Ana runs a bakery. In a day she can bake loaves or cakes, and the two choices fill the same day. Price a cake in loaves, the way the potter's vase was priced.

Now put a second potter next to the first. Jo can make 4 bowls or 2 vases in a day, while the first potter, Mo, makes 9 bowls or 3 vases. Mo is quicker at both jobs. Being able to make more of a good with the same time is called an absolute advantage, and Mo has it in bowls and in vases.

It looks as if Mo should do everything, but look at the prices. A vase costs Mo 3 bowls and costs Jo 4 ÷ 2 = 2 bowls. Jo gives up fewer bowls for each vase, and giving up less is what makes a job cheap. Whoever has the lower opportunity cost of a good has the comparative advantage in it, so Jo has the comparative advantage in vases.

afterFigure.text: Bowls work the other way round. A bowl costs Mo a third of a vase and costs Jo half of one, so Mo has the comparative advantage in bowls. Between two people, each ends up with one of the two jobs, even though one of them is quicker at both.

lead.text: Back to the bakery. Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes a day, and Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Ana is quicker at both jobs, so compare what each baker gives up for one cake.

reveal.text: You compared opportunity costs. A cake costs Ben 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 loaves and Ana 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so the quicker baker is the dearer one.

steps.headline: Ana bakes 12 loaves or 6 cakes a day; Ben bakes 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Who should bake what?

workedSteps.text: Price a cake in loaves for each baker.
Price a loaf in cakes for each baker.
Give each job to the lower cost: Ben bakes the cakes, Ana bakes the loaves.

lead.text: Knowing who should do which job is only half of it. The gain arrives when each person concentrates on their own job and the two of them swap. Go back to the potters. Suppose Jo makes only vases and Mo makes only bowls, and then Mo pays Jo 2.5 bowls for each vase.

Look at Jo first. Making a vase costs Jo 2 bowls, and Jo is now paid 2.5 bowls for it, so each vase leaves Jo half a bowl ahead. Mo is better off too. Making a vase would cost Mo 3 bowls, and buying one from Jo costs only 2.5, which saves half a bowl a vase.

afterFigure.text: Neither potter has done anything harder than before. They have only moved each job to the person who finds it cheaper, and the saving shows up for both of them.

diagram.alt: Jo and Mo drawn as two boxes. A vase goes from Jo to Mo and 2.5 bowls go back. Under each box is the saving: half a bowl ahead for Jo and half a bowl saved for Mo.
diagram.caption: At 2.5 bowls a vase, each potter gains half a bowl a vase.

lead.text: The price of 2.5 bowls worked, but other prices could have worked as well. A seller gains from a swap when the price is above what making the good costs them, and a buyer gains when the price is below what making it would cost them. Both are true only between the two opportunity costs.

For the vases, Jo's cost is 2 bowls and Mo's is 3. At a price of 1.5, Jo would lose by selling and would refuse. At a price of 3.5, Mo would do better making the vases without Jo. Anywhere between 2 and 3 helps them both. Close to 2 most of the gain goes to Mo, and close to 3 most of it goes to Jo.

afterFigure.text: The same holds for any pair. Find each side's cost of the good, and every price between the two costs makes both better off.

diagram.alt: A number line for the price of one vase in bowls, from 1 to 4, with Jo's cost at 2 and Mo's at 3. The stretch between them is marked as the range where both gain.
diagram.caption: Only prices between the two costs help both. Use the buttons to try a price below, inside and above that range.

steps.headline: Ben bakes only cakes and swaps 2 of them with Ana at 1.75 loaves each. Does he come out ahead?

workedSteps.text: Before the swap Ben splits his day, so he makes 2 cakes and 3 loaves.
Now he bakes 4 cakes, keeps 2 and swaps 2 away.
Compare with the 3 loaves he used to bake.

lead.text: Ben's cake costs him 1.5 loaves to make and Ana's costs her 2, and they will swap cakes for loaves. Pick the price, in loaves per cake, that leaves both of them better off.
Mira and Tom share a studio and can code web pages or write reports. Start with Tom and find what he gives up for each page he codes.

reveal.text: Tom gives up 4 reports per page and Mira only 2, so Mira has the comparative advantage in pages.

lead.text: Every swap so far rested on one fact. The two people give up different amounts for the same good, and the difference opens a range of prices between their costs. Inside that range both sides gain, whichever of them is the quicker worker.

Suppose instead that the costs match. If two bakers each give up the same number of loaves for a cake, a seller gains only above that number and a buyer gains only below it, so no price satisfies both. Being twice as quick at every job changes nothing here, because speed multiplies both of a baker's outputs together and leaves the price of one in terms of the other where it was.

afterFigure.text: So the question to ask of any pair is whether their opportunity costs differ. Speed does not answer it.

lead.text: Cara is twice as productive as Dan at both jobs, which is a large absolute advantage. Check whether that makes a swap worthwhile for them.

reveal.text: Equal costs leave no price that helps both sides. Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from differences in productivity.

lesson.orientation: Find comparative advantage from opportunity costs and show that specialisation and trade benefit both sides.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Ana and Ben run bakeries on the same street. In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes, and Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Ana is quicker at both jobs.

That seems to settle things. If Ana can out-bake Ben at everything, she might as well bake everything herself. Yet the two of them would usually do better by splitting the work and swapping. That raises a puzzle: how can the slower baker have anything to offer the quicker one?

The last lesson priced a choice by what it gives up. That same idea answers the puzzle. We'll price each baker's cake in loaves, work out who should bake what, and find the prices at which a swap helps them both.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say who should make what, and show that trade can leave both sides better off.

recap.keyIdea: Comparative advantage belongs to whoever gives up less. Specialise where your cost is lower and trade at a price between the two costs, and both sides gain.

blocks.text: Back at the two bakeries, the puzzle has an answer. Ben's cake costs him 1.5 loaves against Ana's 2, so the slower baker holds the advantage in cakes. A swap at 1.75 loaves left Ben half a loaf ahead, and when two bakers gave up the same amount, there was nothing to swap.

recap.nextHook: Prices in the other good are one kind of cost, and the next lesson looks at how a café decides whether one more hour or one more slice is worth its cost.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes. What is her opportunity cost of one cake, in loaves?
hints: A day of cakes and a day of bread use the same time.
Ask how much bread one cake's share of the day could have made.
Divide her loaves per day by her cakes per day.
questions.onCorrect: 2 loaves. A cake's opportunity cost is the loaves the same time could have made: 12 ÷ 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every loaf her day could make. One cake uses only its share of the day.
That is the most cakes she can bake. The question asks how many loaves one cake replaces.
That is a loaf's cost in cakes, the wrong way up.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes; Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Who gives up fewer loaves to bake a cake? Give the name.
hints: Price a cake in loaves for each baker.
Ana makes more cakes, but ask what each one gives up.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben. A cake costs him 1.5 loaves against Ana's 2.

questions.onCorrect: Ben. A cake costs him 6 ÷ 4 loaves, less than Ana's 12 ÷ 6.

misconceptions.feedback: Ana bakes more cakes, but the question is about what she gives up. Price a cake in loaves for each baker.

questions.prompt: How many more loaves does he end with than before?
hints: Find how many loaves the swap brings him.
He keeps the same number of cakes as before.
Subtract the loaves he used to bake from the loaves he receives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: He receives 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 loaves and keeps 2 cakes, so he has 3.5 − 3 = 0.5 loaves more.

questions.onCorrect: 0.5 loaves more. He keeps the same 2 cakes and ends with 3.5 loaves instead of 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is all the loaves he receives. Take off the 3 he used to bake.
That is the price of one cake. He swaps two, and he already had loaves before.

questions.prompt: Cara can bake 8 loaves or 4 cakes a day; Dan can bake 4 loaves or 2 cakes. By how many loaves does their opportunity cost of a cake differ?
hints: Work out each person's loaves per cake.
Compare the two rates.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each gives up 8 ÷ 4 = 4 ÷ 2 loaves per cake, so the costs are equal and the difference is nothing.

questions.onCorrect: None. Both give up 2 loaves per cake, so no price can leave both better off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each person's cost, not the difference between the costs.
That is how many cakes Cara can bake. Compare the loaves each gives up per cake.

questions.prompt: In an hour Mira can code 4 web pages or write 8 reports. Tom can code 1 page or write 4 reports. What is Tom's opportunity cost of one page, in reports?
hints: Use only Tom's two figures.
Ask how many reports he forgoes to spend an hour on pages.
Divide his reports per hour by his pages per hour.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tom gives up 4 reports ÷ 1 page = 4 reports per page; Mira gives up only 2.

questions.onCorrect: 4 reports. Tom's cost of a page is the reports his hour could have produced: 4 ÷ 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is pages per report, the wrong way up.
That is Mira's cost of a page. The question asks about Tom.
The goods trade at a ratio, so subtracting does not work. Divide instead.

questions.prompt: Mira gives up 2 reports per web page; Tom gives up 4. Which division of work produces gains from trade?
hints: Give each task to the person who gives up less to do it.

acceptedIdeas: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mira has the lower opportunity cost of pages, so she codes them; Tom's lower cost of reports makes him the report writer.

choices.label: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports
Tom codes pages and Mira writes reports

questions.onCorrect: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports: each does the job they give up less for, and both gain from trade.

misconceptions.feedback: Tom gives up more reports for each page, so he is the dearer coder. Give each job to whoever gives up less.
Splitting the hour equally ignores who is cheaper at each job. Gains come from specialising.

questions.prompt: Cleo can bake 2 cakes or 10 loaves in a day. Dev can bake 4 cakes or 4 loaves. Who has the comparative advantage in cakes?

choices.label: Neither: their costs are the same

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dev. A cake costs him 1 loaf and costs Cleo 5.

hints: Price a cake in loaves for each of them.
questions.onCorrect: Dev. A cake costs him 4 ÷ 4 loaves against Cleo's 10 ÷ 2: the lower opportunity cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Baking more loaves makes Cleo's loaves cheap, not her cakes. Compare what each gives up per cake.
Work out each person's loaves per cake. The two costs are far apart.

questions.prompt: Why does Ana end up with the comparative advantage in loaves?

choices.label: A loaf costs her fewer cakes than it costs Ben.
She is faster at baking everything.

acceptedIdeas: A loaf costs her fewer cakes than it costs Ben.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A loaf costs Ana half a cake and Ben two-thirds of one, so her cost is lower.

hints: Compare what each gives up per loaf.
questions.onCorrect: A loaf costs Ana half a cake and Ben two-thirds of one, so her cost is lower.

misconceptions.feedback: Being faster at both is an absolute advantage. Comparative advantage compares what each gives up.
Ben can bake loaves. He gives up more cakes per loaf than Ana does.

hints: Each cake fetches the agreed price in loaves.
He swaps more than one cake.
Multiply the number of cakes swapped by the price of one.
questions.onCorrect: 3.5 loaves: the number of cakes swapped times the price of each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price of one cake. He swaps two.
That is how many loaves he used to bake himself. The swap brings in a different amount.

questions.prompt: Ben's cake costs him 1.5 loaves to make and Ana's costs her 2. Which price, in loaves per cake, helps both?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1.8 sits between 1.5 and 2: Ana pays less than baking costs her, and Ben is paid more than it costs him.

hints: Each side must do better than making the cake themselves.
questions.onCorrect: 1.8: above Ben's cost and below Ana's, so each does better than going it alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Ben would be paid less than a cake costs him to bake, so he would not sell.
Ana would pay more than baking the cake herself costs her, so she would not buy.

questions.prompt: Lena can make 6 mugs or 24 plates in a day; Sam can make 6 mugs or 6 plates. By how many plates does Lena's opportunity cost of a mug exceed Sam's?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lena: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 plates per mug. Sam: 6 ÷ 6 = 1 plate. 4 − 1 = 3.

hints: Price a mug in plates for Lena.
Do the same for Sam.
Subtract the smaller price from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: 3 plates. Price a mug for each, then take the smaller from the larger.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Lena's price alone. The question asks how much it exceeds Sam's.
That is Sam's price alone. Find how far Lena's price sits above it.
Subtracting the maximums skips the pricing. Price a mug in plates for each person first.

questions.prompt: A cake costs Ana 2 loaves to bake herself and costs Ben 1.5. They agree a price of 1.75 loaves per cake. Ana buys 8 cakes from Ben instead of baking them. How many loaves does she save?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Baking 8 cakes would cost her 8 × 2 = 16 loaves. Buying costs 8 × 1.75 = 14. She saves 16 − 14 = 2.

hints: How many loaves would baking those cakes herself cost her?
How many loaves does she pay Ben for the same cakes?
Subtract what she pays from what baking would have cost.
questions.onCorrect: 2 loaves. She pays less than baking would cost her, on every cake she buys.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what she pays Ben. Compare it with what baking would have cost her.
That is what baking the cakes herself would cost. Subtract what she actually pays.
That is the saving on one cake. She buys several.
